# ripple-pool A Roman marine mosaic seen through a shallow pool of clear water, after Evan Wallace's WebGL Water. A finger or pointer drawn across leaves a wake, a click or tap drops a stone that sends out a train of rings, the rings run to the walls and come back, and on a phone tilting it sloshes the whole basin. Left alone it is still alive: a faint net of sunlight drifts across the floor, the way it does in any shallow pool in the sun. ```html ``` The `` sizes the pool. Leave it at its natural ratio, or give the figure a height and the img `object-fit: cover` (and any `object-position`); the water takes exactly the same crop. `class="rp-bleed"` on the figure makes a full screen of water (`100svh`). Or call `ripplePool(figure, options)` yourself; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-damping` | `damping` | `3.5` | roughly how many seconds a disturbance takes to die away | | `data-strength` | `strength` | `1` | scales every stone, wake and slosh | | `data-rain` | `rain` | `7000` | ms between idle drops (jittered ±40%); `0` = never. The first comes 1.2 s after the pool is seen | | `data-caustics` | `caustics` | `0.7` | 0-1, how strongly the ripples focus light onto the floor | | `data-ambient` | `ambient` | `0.35` | 0-1, the sunlit swell and drifting caustic net when nobody touches it; `0` = off (the water is then perfectly still at rest, every tessera exactly the image) | The options object wins over the attributes. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--rp-tint` | the mosaic's own mean colour, darkened | colour that deeper water (troughs) leans toward | | `--rp-glint` | `#fffaf0` | colour of the specular glint | | `--rp-rim` | a hairline and a soft inset shadow | `box-shadow` where the water meets the edge; `none` to drop it | | `--rp-floor` | `--paper-2` | behind the image while it loads | | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | There is deliberately no blue: the water is clear and the palette is the floor's. ## How it works - **Water.** A height field of about 256 cells on the long side (never finer than 3 css px) is stepped on the CPU at a fixed rate: the wave equation plus a small surface-tension term (the laplacian of the laplacian), so short ripples run ahead and a stone sends a train of rings rather than one, and a touch of viscosity that takes out grid-sized ripples. Walls reflect. The step rate is set from the cell size so waves travel at the same 250 css px/s in a phone or a desktop pool, and stone heights scale with the grid so slopes look the same. - **Texture.** Each frame the slope, light focus and height of every cell are packed into one small RGBA8 texture (128 = flat). No float textures, so it runs on any WebGL1. - **Shader.** The mosaic is pre-cropped (`object-fit` honoured) into a texture at one texel per device pixel, so at rest it is sampled exactly. The floor is sampled where a ray bent by the surface lands; caustics are `1 / det(I + k · Hessian(h))`, the area a patch of light shrinks or grows to; a soft fixed light glints only off facets steep enough to catch it; troughs lean a little toward the depth tint. - **Ambient swell.** Not simulated: five long, slow analytic waves in the shader. Their exact Hessian goes through the same `1 / det(I + kH)`, which gives the wobbly net of bright folds and dim cells, plus a pixel or two of refraction. Drawn at about 30 fps. - **Light is tone-mapped** both ways (`1 - exp(-kx)`), with a shoulder above 0.78 and less added light on pale stones, so bright bands warm white tesserae instead of burning them out, and the dimmed side carries contrast. - **Wake.** The pointer is something pressed into the water to a fixed depth and drawn along (the water under it is pulled toward that depth, never past it), so a slow hand makes a gentle wake, a fast one a V, and neither runs away. - **Stone.** A Gaussian-windowed cosine (crater, lip, fainter second trough), then the rebound and a smaller bob: it leaves as a train of three or four rings that spread past a third of the pool and come back off the walls. Stone radius is 3.4% of the pool's long side (14-56 px), and a small pool gets a proportionally gentler splash. - **Tilt.** The change of tilt is added to the surface as a ramp; the walls turn it into a wave that runs across and back (`tilt.js`, shared, smoothed). ## Tuning The constants at the top of `ripple-pool.js` are the physics: `WAVE` (speed), `TENSION` (how much a stone rings), `VISCOSITY`, `REFRACT` (how far the floor shifts, css px at the steepest slope), `FOCUS_K` (how hard light focuses). The ambient net's wavelengths, speeds and fold depth (`f`) are in `swell()` in the shader; shorter wavelengths make smaller cells. Busy, high-contrast mosaics show the water best. A mosaic photographed at around one tessera per 15-30 px of screen is ideal; the full-bleed demo image is 3840 px wide so a 3x phone gets it nearly 1:1. ## Behaviour and cost - **Ambient costs a light continuous loop while the pool is visible**: one full-screen draw about 30 times a second, no simulation (the sim only runs while the water is disturbed). Off screen or in a hidden tab, nothing runs. - With `data-ambient="0"` the loop stops entirely once the water is still: the last faint shimmer settles quickly, about 6 s after the last touch. Rain waits on a `setTimeout`, not a loop, and pauses off screen and in a hidden tab. - Canvas DPR is capped at 2, **except** on a 3x phone when the pool stays under ~3.4 megapixels (a full-screen 390x844 pool is 3.0), because the tesserae must be as sharp as the plain ``. - The simulation costs well under a couple of ms a frame on a laptop; the shader is six texture reads and five sines a pixel. - Without WebGL, or if the image is cross-origin (WebGL refuses it), the `` simply stays. If the GPU drops the context, the img shows again until it comes back. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The image is decorative (`alt=""`); the canvas is `aria-hidden`. - With motion allowed the figure becomes focusable (`role="button"`, a default `aria-label` unless you set one): Enter or Space drops a stone, the arrow keys draw a wake across. Focus shows an accent ring. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: the mosaic under a faint, frozen surface (two gentle rings caught part way out) and a frozen net of light. Nothing moves, there is no ambient loop and no rain, and touch does nothing. - Touch scrolling is never blocked: the page scrolls over the pool as usual, and a finger resting on it as it scrolls past leaves a wake. - Print shows the plain image. ## Credits - After Evan Wallace's [WebGL Water](https://madebyevan.com/webgl-water/); no code from it is used. - Images from Wikimedia Commons, see `assets/credits.json` (Milreu frigidarium: Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0; Naples fish and ducks: public domain).
